paragraphs: The question “What, absolutely, is the best government?” cannot be answered, and is also indeterminate; or rather, there are as many good answers as there are possible combinations of the absolute and relative situations of all nations.
But if it is asked by what sign we can tell whether a given people is well or badly governed, that is another matter, and since it is a question of fact, it admits of an answer.

Yet it is not answered, because everyone wants to answer it in his own way. Subjects extol public tranquility, citizens individual liberty; the one class prefers security of possessions, the other security of person; the one regards the most severe government as the best, the other maintains that the mildest is best; the one wants crimes punished, the other wants them prevented; the one wants the State to be feared by its neighbors, the other prefers that it be ignored; the one is content if money circulates, the other demands that the people have bread. Even if agreement were reached on these and similar points, should we have got any further? Since moral qualities do not admit of exact measurement, agreement about the mark does not mean agreement about its valuation.

For my part, I am continually astonished that so simple a mark is not recognized, or that men are so dishonest as not to admit it. What is the purpose of political association? The preservation and prosperity of its members. And what is the surest mark of their preservation and prosperity? Their numbers and population. Look nowhere else, then, for this disputed mark. Other things being equal, the government under which the citizens increase and multiply most, without outside help, without naturalization or colonies, is beyond question the best. The government under which a people dwindles and diminishes is the worst. Calculators, it is left to you to count, to measure, to compare.[1]

the preference for human prosperity. Those in which letters and the arts have flourished have been admired too much, because the hidden purpose of their cultivation has not been fathomed, and their fatal effects have not been taken into account. “Idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset.” [“Fools called ‘humanity’ what was a part of slavery,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] Shall we never see, in the maxims that books lay down, the crude self-interest that makes their authors speak? No: whatever they may say, when a country is losing its population, despite its renown, it is not true that all is well, and it is not enough for a poet to have an income of 100,000 francs to make his age the best of all. We should pay less attention to the apparent calm and tranquility of the rulers than to the well-being of whole nations, and above all of the most populous States. A hailstorm lays waste several cantons, but it rarely causes a famine. Uprisings and civil wars give rulers rude shocks, but they are not the real ills of peoples, who may even get a respite while there is a dispute over who shall tyrannize them. Their true prosperity and their calamities come from their lasting condition. It is when the whole remains crushed beneath the yoke that decay sets in, and that the rulers destroy them at will, and “ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant” [“Where they create solitude, they call it peace,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] When the quarrels of the great disturbed the kingdom of France, and the Coadjutor of Paris carried a dagger in his pocket to the Parliament, none of this kept the people of France from prospering and multiplying in dignity, ease and freedom. Long ago Greece flourished in the midst of the most savage wars; blood ran in torrents, and yet the whole country was covered with inhabitants. It seemed, says Machiavelli, that in the midst of murder, proscription and civil war, our republic only thrived: the virtue, morals and independence of its citizens did more to strengthen it than all their dissensions did to weaken it. A little disturbance gives the soul elasticity; what makes the race truly prosperous is not so much peace as liberty.
